channel.title: Signal Brief · Quantum
channel.description: Signal Brief: the day in technology, in The Signal's own words. Every item is written from linked official sources and fact checked before publication.

item.title: Cleveland Clinic, RIKEN and IBM simulate drug binding across 12,000 atoms
item.description: A collaboration between Cleveland Clinic, RIKEN and IBM has run a hybrid quantum-classical simulation of full protein-ligand complexes exceeding 12,000 atoms, described as the largest such calculation to date. The team paired two 156-qubit IBM Heron r2 processors with three supercomputers, collecting 3.0 billion measurement shots across 21,006 circuits, and reported up to a 210-fold improvement in fragment energy accuracy over earlier quantum-embedding benchmarks. The work, detailed in a preprint, produced a binding energy prediction for a T4-lysozyme complex. Why it matters for tech: Drug binding predictions at this scale move quantum computing closer to real pharmaceutical work, where accurate energies decide which molecules advance.

item.title: A cheaper way to hunt for diamond qubits
item.description: A researcher at the US Department of Energy's Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory has developed a method that cuts the cost of modelling quantum defects in diamond, by treating a cluster of just 16 to 30 atoms around a defect as a separate molecule. The approach, published in ACS Central Science, already identified promising new qubit candidates involving boron and oxygen defects, which emit ultraviolet and blue light respectively, unlike the well-known nitrogen-vacancy centre that emits red. Because each defect type responds to different light, several kinds could be combined in one device and addressed independently. Why it matters for tech: Cheaper screening of diamond defects widens the search for qubits that work at room temperature, which would simplify quantum hardware.

item.title: PsiQuantum and AMD widen their partnership to build the classical side of fault-tolerant quantum computers
item.description: PsiQuantum and AMD have expanded their partnership to co-design the computing infrastructure for utility-scale, fault-tolerant quantum machines and the hybrid workloads that mix quantum, high-performance and AI computing. The work moves beyond AMD Versal FPGAs to Instinct GPUs, EPYC CPUs and the ROCm software stack, paired with PsiQuantum's silicon photonics platform, and AMD also plans an equity investment in PsiQuantum. The first focus is pharmaceutical research and drug discovery, and the companies will share more at the SC26 conference in Chicago from November 15 to 20. Why it matters for tech: Fault-tolerant machines will need as much classical computing around them as quantum hardware inside, so chipmakers are now part of the quantum build.

item.title: Qunova's hybrid method matches the best classical result on a hard chemistry problem
item.description: Qunova Computing says its HI-VQE algorithm reached chemical accuracy in an 80-qubit simulation of the 4Fe-4S iron-sulfur cluster, using an IBM Quantum System Two machine at RIKEN alongside the Fugaku supercomputer. Its ground-state energy estimate of minus 327.2482 Hartree agreed within chemical accuracy with the leading classical reference, calculated by the Density Matrix Renormalization Group method at minus 327.2471 Hartree. The workflow also used about 300 times fewer Fugaku node-hours than a previously published sample-based quantum diagonalization approach on the same molecule. Why it matters for tech: A quantum workflow that agrees with the reference classical calculation on a benchmark molecule gives chemists a reason to trust hybrid methods for real design questions.

item.title: IBM details Nighthawk r3 chip and a 1,040-qubit system for 2027
item.description: IBM has announced Nighthawk r3, a processor designed to run 10,000 quantum operations across 520 programmable qubits, with 2,034 physical qubits in total. IBM plans to link two r3 processors into a single 1,040-qubit system in 2027, using chip to chip interconnects it has already demonstrated. The current Nighthawk r2 runs up to 100,000 samples a second and more than 7,500 operations on 120 qubits, and partners have run 34 billion circuits on it so far. Why it matters for tech: Linking processors with chip to chip interconnects is IBM's route to larger systems without building one giant chip, and sample speed decides whether heavy workloads finish in practical time.

item.title: Rigetti reports third-quarter revenue of $1.4 million and a 99.5% fidelity milestone
item.description: Rigetti reported third-quarter revenue of $1.4 million, with nine-month revenue of $10.9 million, up about 110% on a year earlier, and an operating loss of $33.2 million. The company ended the quarter with $497.1 million in cash and investments and no debt. Its Cepheus-1-108Q system reached 99.5% median two-qubit gate fidelity, Rigetti signed a definitive agreement for up to $100 million from the US Department of Commerce under the CHIPS Act, and it targets a 300-plus-qubit system at about 99.7% fidelity by mid-2028. Why it matters for tech: The fidelity figure and the federal award show a small quantum hardware maker funding its roadmap from both sales growth and government research money.

item.title: Quantinuum and RIKEN complete the Reimei upgrade to the H2 system
item.description: Quantinuum and RIKEN have completed the upgrade of the Reimei quantum computer at RIKEN to Quantinuum's System Model H2, and expanded their partnership around quantum-AI hybrid supercomputing in Japan. The upgraded machine sits alongside RIKEN's Fugaku supercomputer and the ROQUO GPU system, and the partners have started two research projects on it, one training an AI model on quantum data for magnetism simulations and one simulating a light-absorbing biomolecule. Under a separate agreement with SoftBank, the partners will study connecting quantum computers directly with AI data centres in Japan. Why it matters for tech: A working three-way hybrid of quantum, supercomputing and AI hardware gives researchers a live platform for testing whether quantum-generated data improves AI models for materials and biology.

item.title: Xanadu and HyperLight cut photonic switch loss to 7 millidecibels
item.description: Xanadu and HyperLight have reported an optical switch insertion loss of 7 millidecibels using thin-film lithium niobate technology, down from 20 millidecibels in their previous result in 2025. Lower switch loss reduces the degradation of quantum signals as they pass through the switches that route light in a photonic quantum computer. The result was demonstrated on HyperLight's thin-film lithium niobate chiplet platform, which the companies describe as a high-volume wafer manufacturing line. Why it matters for tech: Switch loss is one of the physical limits on scaling photonic quantum computers, so a measured drop of nearly two-thirds changes the overhead budget for larger machines built on this platform.

item.title: Diraq installs an 8-qubit silicon spin computer in a Sydney data centre
item.description: Diraq has installed an 8-qubit silicon spin quantum computer at Equinix's data centre in Sydney, which the company describes as the first such system inside a commercial data centre. The system uses under 20 kilowatts and 170 square feet, and Diraq plans to reach up to 256 qubits in the same system within a year. Diraq also published a Quantum at Work report estimating that a 10 percentage point rise in clinical trial success rates could save about $600 million per medicine. Why it matters for tech: Running a quantum system inside a commercial data centre tests whether the technology can operate as a hosted service alongside ordinary cloud hardware instead of in a laboratory.

item.title: IonQ and Carahsoft partner to sell quantum systems to the public sector
item.description: IonQ and Carahsoft have announced a strategic partnership in which Carahsoft becomes IonQ's distributor for the public sector, handling procurement, contract vehicles and resale to federal agencies, higher education and state and local government. The agreement covers quantum computing, networking, sensing and security, and cites Executive Order 14413 on quantum innovation. IonQ points to its Stage C progress in DARPA's Quantum Benchmarking Initiative and its quantum network work with the Air Force Research Laboratory in Rome, New York. Why it matters for tech: A dedicated public sector channel puts IonQ's systems in front of government buyers through established procurement routes, which is how most government quantum purchases are made.

item.title: Riverlane cuts surface-code logical errors with data-driven decoder fix
item.description: Riverlane has demonstrated a method that finds unmodelled correlated errors directly from syndrome measurement data and folds them into the detector error models used to decode surface-code qubits. The augmented models cut logical error rates by up to 75% in simulations and by 14% on Google's published superconducting hardware data. The approach stays compatible with fast graph-based decoders such as PyMatching, which existing error-correction pipelines already use. Why it matters for tech: Better decoding from measured noise, rather than from theory alone, moves error-corrected quantum computing forward without waiting on new hardware.

item.title: IBM unveils Quantum System Two at the University of Chicago
item.description: IBM, the University of Chicago, the State of Illinois and the Illinois Quantum and Microelectronics Park have unveiled an IBM Quantum System Two in Chicago, the company's first quantum computer in Illinois. The system runs on IBM's Nighthawk processor, a 120-qubit chip, and is hosted at the university's Hyde Park Labs. It anchors the National Quantum Algorithm Center, where researchers from universities, labs and companies work on practical quantum applications, and will move to the new Illinois Quantum and Microelectronics Park campus once it is built. Why it matters for tech: Putting a 120-qubit system on a university campus gives Illinois researchers local hardware for algorithm work instead of remote cloud access.

item.title: Oxford team simulates Aharonov-Bohm effect with two trapped ions
item.description: Researchers at the University of Oxford have simulated the Aharonov-Bohm effect in a lattice gauge theory using a hybrid trapped-ion quantum computer, in a study published in Nature Physics. Two trapped ions formed a loop with two paths, and entangling the qubits that encode the magnetic flux changed whether a particle could tunnel between sites. When the entangled qubits encoded a nonzero flux, the two paths cancelled out and tunnelling stopped entirely, showing the simulation captures how flux affects particle motion. Why it matters for tech: Simulating gauge theories with matter and flux together moves quantum simulation closer to the physics behind particle interactions and exotic materials.

item.title: AI assisted proof settles a 2008 question about quantum speedups
item.description: A proof by David Turturean of Physical Superintelligence has settled the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, open since 2008, which asks when quantum computers can gain dramatic advantages over classical machines. The proof shows that for yes or no questions on most randomly generated inputs, a classical algorithm can estimate a quantum algorithm’s answer without needing vastly more reads of the input, so large speedups need structure in the problem. The proof was found by an AI research system using a non public Anthropic model on the third day of a run, then checked in the Lean proof assistant and reviewed by researchers. Why it matters for tech: It draws a clearer line around where quantum advantage can come from, pointing algorithm research toward problems with structure worth exploiting.

item.title: UK announces fresh funding to speed up quantum commercialisation
item.description: The UK government and UK Research and Innovation have announced new funding to speed up quantum commercialisation, including £138 million for quantum sensing procurement across government, £12 million for a national commercialisation skills centre and £35 million for quantum networking testbeds. The skills centre will be run by the UK Quantum SuperConnector, a partnership led by Imperial College London with Bristol, Cambridge, Glasgow and Oxford. A UKRI review of £300 million invested between 2014 and 2024 found it helped create more than 2,000 skilled jobs, supported 74 spinout companies and attracted £482 million in private investment. Why it matters for tech: Public money is now aimed at turning research into products and jobs, and the UK is measuring a decade of funding by the companies and skills it produced.

item.title: Quantinuum maps its Nexus platform toward a fault tolerant computer in 2029
item.description: Quantinuum published a roadmap to grow Nexus, its platform as a service, into a developer platform for fault tolerant quantum applications, tracking hardware releases through Apollo, its planned universal fault tolerant computer in 2029. Releases will progressively automate error correction, resource management and deployment. Nexus already serves more than 200 organisations, up 45% in 2026, with job submissions up tenfold in the year to August 2026. Why it matters for tech: Quantum vendors are now competing on developer platforms, not only hardware, so applications built today can carry over to fault tolerant machines.

item.title: IBM, Oak Ridge and AMD pair quantum hardware with supercomputing to advance error correction
item.description: IBM, the Quantum Science Center at Oak Ridge National Laboratory and AMD launched a joint co-design platform for quantum error correction, combining quantum and high performance computing. The first deployment pairs IBM quantum computers, including the 120 qubit Nighthawk processor, with Oak Ridge's Umbra system, powered by AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs and 5th Gen EPYC CPUs. The work supports the US Department of Energy goal of 100 logical qubits running 100,000 hard operations by late 2028. Why it matters for tech: Error correction needs classical computing at scale, and this platform tests quantum and supercomputing as one system rather than two separate tools.

item.title: IBM Quantum and QuICS use AI agents to find over 500 magic state factory designs
item.description: IBM Quantum and University of Maryland QuICS researchers used AI agents with deterministic solvers to discover more than 500 new magic state factories. These produce the non Clifford states that fault tolerant quantum computers need, with significantly lower resource requirements, and the detailed circuit models are openly accessible. Why it matters for tech: Magic state production is a major cost centre in fault tolerant designs, so cheaper factories change machine economics.

item.title: Superinductor built inside a silicon chip in a commercial CMOS process
item.description: A study in Nature Electronics by researchers from nanoGUNE's Quantum Hardware group, Quantum Motion and UK partners introduces a superinductor created within a silicon integrated circuit. The device was fabricated in a commercial CMOS process, the same family of processes used for ordinary chips. Why it matters for tech: Components made in standard chip processes are easier to manufacture at scale for quantum hardware.

item.title: Universal Quantum unveils a foundry made trapped ion processor built for modular scaling
item.description: Universal Quantum has launched the iQPU, a trapped ion processor fabricated in a foundry, with control electronics integrated on chip. Its UQConnect interconnect is designed to link multiple modules, and the processors are destined for two quantum computers being built for the German Aerospace Center. Why it matters for tech: Foundry fabrication and modular links are two of the practical steps needed to scale trapped ion machines.

item.title: One extra measurement cuts qubit errors by more than half in Regensburg experiment
item.description: Researchers at the University of Regensburg and their international partners showed that a single additional measurement before a series of quantum operations reduced the qubit error rate by more than half. The results were published in Applied Physics Reviews. Why it matters for tech: Low cost error reduction matters because error correction overhead decides how large a useful quantum machine must be.

item.title: Experiment backs a route to more error resistant quantum information storage
item.description: Researchers have produced experimental support for the theoretical basis of topological quantum computing, an approach that stores information in special quantum states expected to be more resistant to local disturbances. The work addresses one of the field's core problems: how easily quantum information degrades. Why it matters for tech: If topological approaches hold up, they could reduce the error correction burden that dominates quantum hardware design today.
